Let’s Build a Brain
pinboard.description:
In this article, we’ll build a tiny creature called a spark, and we’ll give it a very simple brain. As you’ll see, even this tiny brain can create rich and unexpected behaviors.

Light eaters
Suppose this spark feeds on light. Its goal in life is to reach the light.

The light-hungry spark needs a way to sense the world. So we’ll give it a rudimentary eye — a single neuron that detects brightness and converts it into electrical pulses.

It also needs a way to move. So we’ll give it another neuron that can wiggle a flipper.

pinboard.title: An Ancient Virus Explains Why the Human Brain Is Special
pinboard.description:
Scientists have discovered a family of retroviruses that invaded the genomes of chimps and other primates, silencing genes involved with brain development, while humans were left unaffected.
Your brain on viral content 
Gerdes, Patricia; Karlsson, Ofelia; Garza, Raquel; Atacho, Diahann A. M. et al. “Retroviral insertions contributed to the divergence of human and chimpanzee brains.” Science Advances.
A virus that infected chimpanzees millions of years ago shaped the divergence of human and chimp brain development, shedding light on how our own species came to be more cognitively complex than our closest living relatives, according to a new study. 
Retroviruses are infectious agents that can invade the genomes of their hosts and insert copies of their own genetic material, producing long-term evolutionary effects. Researchers have now discovered a family of these endogenous retroviruses called PTERV1—which are abundant in chimpanzees, but absent in humans—that influence brain development.   
“Among primates, the human brain stands out as the largest and most complex due in part to an increase in cortical neurons and increase in synaptic connectivity,” said a team led by researchers from Lund University. “With a size roughly three times that of our closest living evolutionary relative, the chimpanzee, it has unique cognitive capabilities.”
“The underlying genetic divergences responsible for these differences are still poorly understood,” the researchers continued, noting that their new findings “reveal a mechanism by which endogenous retroviral insertions contributed to human-chimpanzee brain divergence.”
The team discovered the mechanism using human and chimpanzee brain organoids, which are miniature clusters of neurons grown from stem cells that can model some aspects of brain development. The results revealed chimpanzee-specific PTERV1 insertions on chromosome 19 that silences a gene called LINC00662. In contrast, this gene is active during human brain development, and affects neuronal maturation, development, and outgrowth.  
“These PTERV1 insertions are thought to have originated from infections that occurred in the ancestors of African apes about 5 to 7 million years ago,” said the team. “PTERV1 elements are found in chimpanzees, bonobos, and gorillas…Notably, the absence of PTERV1 insertions from the human genome suggests that either the human and chimpanzee lineages did not occupy the same habitat at the time or that germline-competent cells of the human ancestor were resistant to this infection.”
“In summary, this study describes how retroviral insertions contributed to the functional divergence of the human and chimpanzee brain, providing a mechanism by which retroviral infections influenced primate brain speciation,” they added.
In other words, early humans appear to have dodged consequential pandemics that widely infected our primate brethren simply because they had a random immunity to it, or roamed different ranges. While retroviruses are far from the only factor in our cognitive development, it’s still eerie to think that our human brain—that brilliant lump you are using to read these words—is shaped by dumb luck.

pinboard.title: No one paid me to disagree with Jonathan Haidt. It was teenagers who taught me that he was wrong.
pinboard.description:
Unbeknownst to me, some of Richard Blumenthal’s ardent supporters for his Senatorial campaign were outraged that I dared to challenge the politician’s arguments about internet safety. They were determined to prove that I was falsifying data on behalf of the tech industry. The Frontline reporter told me she was assigned to uncover my duplicitousness. She had concluded I hadn’t done anything but report on the scientific insights of the field. She spiked the story, but she warned me that I had pissed off some very powerful people and I would probably have to deal with being demonized going forward for standing up for research. Ugh.
----
Cuz here’s the thing… It IS possible to despise the tech companies AND understand why teenagers use their products and find value from doing so. Listen to teenagers; they get these contradictions. Their hatred of the tech companies is growing exponentially even as they use the tools those companies provide. (You should see their attitudes towards AI companies. Oooh-whee…) It’s also possible to care about kids’ mental health AND think that the solution doesn’t start and stop with tech. And it’s possible to do rigorous research AND discover that tech isn’t the biggest monster in teens’ lives that anti-tech advocates think it is.

pinboard.title: Galactus the Devourer - by Ben Recht - arg min
pinboard.description:
"Indeed, in the case of OpenAI’s new algorithm for the satisfiability problem, the bound was
\[
n^d 2^{\frac{Cn\log{\log{n}}}{\sqrt{\log{n}}}}
\]
For some unspecified constant numbers d and C. Ugly as this expression is, this was touted on Twitter as the biggest moment in theoretical computer science in 50 years. It was covered all over the tech press this week. OpenAI clearly wanted us to think it was a big fucking deal. And many theoretical computer scientists took to social media to agree.
"Since it was such a big deal, I wanted to see if I could understand the algorithm a bit. Of course, as I’ve told all of you, we’re not supposed to read these papers. We’re supposed to ask ChatGPT what they say. And ChatGPT told me there was a catch.
"The derived algorithm runs exhaustive search—the algorithm Edmonds declared bad in 1965—if the number of variables is less than 10^10,000,000,000,000,000,000,000,000.
"This is a completely unfathomable number.3 There are something like 10^80 atoms in the universe. That’s 10^9,999,999,999,999,999,999,999,920 times smaller. Up until this barely finite threshold, the magic new algorithm calls an exponential-time subroutine. For any problem that we could ever consider, the procedure is exponential time. The “result” is that only in some bizarre, unknowable neighborhood of infinity, satisfiability problems are solved in subexponential time."
